planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Quickfire blooms several weeks earlier than most panicle hydrangeas, with white flowers that begin turning pink to deep rose in midsummer rather than fall.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Quickfire earns its name by flowering several weeks ahead of most other panicle hydrangeas, opening white conical flower clusters in early summer that gradually age to deep pink and finally rich rose-red as the season progresses, giving a longer overall season of color than later-blooming types. Unlike mophead hydrangea, panicle types like Quickfire bloom on new wood, so a hard pruning in late winter does not sacrifice the coming season's flowers and instead encourages a strong flush of new flowering stems. Its sturdy stems hold the flower clusters upright well even in rain, and the plant tolerates more sun and drier soil than mophead hydrangeas once established.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Fire Light was bred for exceptionally strong, sturdy stems that hold its large flower clusters upright without flopping, even after heavy rain.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Fire Light was bred specifically to solve the floppy-stem problem common in many panicle hydrangea cultivars, holding its large, dense, white flower clusters proudly upright even as they age and turn deep red-pink in late summer and fall. Like other panicle hydrangeas it blooms reliably on new wood, so a hard renewal pruning in late winter does not sacrifice the season's flowers. It tolerates more sun and less consistent moisture than mophead hydrangeas once established, and the sturdy stems make it a good choice for a mixed border where less rigid hydrangea cultivars tend to sprawl after rain.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Invincibelle Spirit was the first pink-flowered selection of native smooth hydrangea, a species traditionally available only in white.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Invincibelle Spirit was a breakthrough introduction as the first pink-blooming cultivar of native smooth hydrangea (the species behind the classic white Annabelle), producing rounded clusters of soft pink flowers on a native plant traditionally available only in white. Like Annabelle, it blooms on new wood, so it can be cut back hard in late winter and still flower reliably the same year, and it rebounds quickly from winter damage in colder zones. Its stems are somewhat sturdier than old Annabelle types but can still benefit from light staking in a very rainy, exposed site. It is a good pollinator plant and, being a native species selection, tends to be adaptable and low-maintenance across a range of soil conditions.

common_name: Pocomoke Crape Myrtle (True Dwarf Groundcover-Type Rose-Pink Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Pocomoke's true dwarf size makes it useful as a low border or mass planting rather than a tree, and it needs little to no annual pruning.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pocomoke is one of the true dwarf National Arboretum crape myrtle selections, staying under three feet tall and wide, useful as a low border, mass planting, or large-scale groundcover rather than the shade-tree role most crape myrtles fill. It produces rich rose-pink flower clusters over a long summer season and, like other National Arboretum hybrids, shows good resistance to powdery mildew. Its very small mature size means it needs almost no pruning beyond removing dead wood, in sharp contrast to the standard practice of cutting back larger crape myrtles.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Arboretum Crape Myrtle Program

common_name: Cheyenne Crape Myrtle (Semi-Dwarf True Red Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Cheyenne's compact size and true red flower color make it a popular choice for smaller foundation plantings.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Cheyenne is valued among National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtles for its true, vivid red flower color, a shade less common among crape myrtle cultivars than the many available pinks, lavenders, and whites. The compact, semi-dwarf size fits foundation plantings and smaller landscapes better than the large tree-form crape myrtles, and it shows good resistance to powdery mildew typical of the National Arboretum breeding program. Fall foliage takes on attractive orange-red tones. Remove root suckers and prune lightly to remove dead or crossing branches rather than heavily topping the plant.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Arboretum Crape Myrtle Program
